pillar_reactions.evidence: The rep tied the pillar to the prospect's own Kinstretch experience — 'you mentioned this program that you were going through about the strength, the joint. That's very aligned with how kettlebell workouts actually perform' — and pitched 3-4 sessions of 30-40 minutes plus 5-10 minute tailored mobility protocols. Asked 'Do you feel like this approach would make sense for you?' the prospect answered only 'Yeah. Okay.' Understood and agreed, no questions and no volunteered enthusiasm.

Presented as what you eat / when you eat / how much you eat, no calorie counting, a 10-to-8-hour window, and one restaurant meal a week — the rep explicitly hooked it to the fried chicken sandwich the prospect had named. Response was 'Sounds good. Yeah.' and no questions when asked.

The prospect pre-sold this pillar himself at 00:03:46 — 'if somebody puts something in front of me and holds me accountable to it, like that is usually a much more helpful way of operating for me' — and when the rep introduced it as 'the one that you were waiting for', he cut in with 'The big one, yeah.' After the weekly check-ins, movement video review and Trevor's direct phone number were described, he said 'No. Sounds great. Well-structured.'

anchors.raw: when I had a personal trainer, I was, well, was paying for Equinox, which was like 250 at the time... 250 a month. And then the personal trainer that I had was, I think it was like two times a week in person, and I was paying about maybe $1,300 a month for that. So this is obviously less than that, but that's kind of my frame of reference here.
anchors.competitor: Equinox membership plus an in-person personal trainer
anchors.note: The prospect did the arithmetic himself and landed on the offer being cheaper than what he used to spend — roughly $1,550/mo historic versus $1,000/mo for the programme. This is the single strongest thing in the call and the rep did nothing with it; he never repeated it back or used it to close the price.

anchors.raw: this was also someone that I had found on Instagram, and I think the guy is fantastic... the program was, it was a self-serve model, so it was like, he wasn't holding me accountable... if you wanted to do the proper lesson, which got the most yield out of it, they were 60 to 90 minutes per session.
anchors.competitor: Kinstretch / joint-specific online program (unnamed instructor, Instagram)
anchors.note: A low-cost self-serve alternative that he says worked well while he did it. It failed on time and accountability, which is exactly the gap the offer fills, so it is a weak anchor — but it establishes that a cheap product can move his mobility needle, and nobody addressed that directly.

anchors.raw: we recently started paying for a nanny, which is, like, many thousands of dollars a month. And just, like, general childcare stuff is very expensive out here.
anchors.note: The real constraint is not perceived value but a newly loaded monthly household budget. This is what the payment-plan option exists for and it was never offered.

unmet_demand.want: Root-cause correction of a 13-year-old shoulder malposition and right-side hip/knee/ankle mechanics — the myofascial-release-plus-strengthen approach he says worked once in LA
unmet_demand.why_unmet: The programme answer is 5-10 minute mobility protocols written by a strength coach and delivered through an app. Nobody said whether that is or is not equivalent to the clinical rehab he is describing, and no clinician is involved at any point.

unmet_demand.want: A monthly payment structure for the $6,000
unmet_demand.why_unmet: He asked 'is there like a monthly plan?' and was told to put it on a credit card. The playbook's own money play says 'for some we break it up', so the capability appears to exist and was not offered.
